findings.title: Recovery codes are written to user storage in plaintext, unlike the local DB path
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generatedCodes list (JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)) and passes that JSON to user storage via updateCredential. The local fallback in the same method persists the credentialModel built by RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...), which stores hashed codes (the codebase verifies codes by hashing input with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode and comparing hashes). So the two storage paths hold different representations of the same secret. With this change, every recovery code is persisted in clear text in an external user store such as LDAP or a custom backend, where anyone with read access to that store can use them to log in. The method also takes both credentialModel and generatedCodes, which lets the two representations diverge. The user-storage path should store the same hashed representation as the local path.

findings.title: Recovery codes validated in user storage are never consumed and can be replayed
findings.body: The recovery-code branch of isValid returns true when the submitted code matches any stored code, but it never marks that code as used or updates the stored credential. The authenticator (RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator) relies on credential.allCodesUsed() to trigger regeneration and to clean up exhausted codes. For a user-storage credential that state never changes, so allCodesUsed() stays false and the same recovery code can be used indefinitely. Single-use semantics are lost for user-storage codes. This is the reference provider for the user-storage contract, so it should consume the matched code, and a test should assert that a used code is rejected.

findings.title: Exhausted user-storage recovery codes are not removed, leaving a broken configured credential
findings.body: The credential is now looked up with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, which prefers the federated credential. Cleanup still calls removeStoredCredentialById, which only operates on the local credential store, so an exhausted federated credential is never removed. The credential therefore still reports configuredFor = true, and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean then calls getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get() on a credential with no unused codes, which throws NoSuchElementException on later logins. The test provider also rebuilds the credential in getCredentials without propagating the stored id (myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()), so the id passed here may not match the stored credential. Removal for federated credentials needs to go through the storage provider, or the exhausted state needs to be handled explicitly.

findings.title: New recovery-code test only covers the happy path
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin sets up codes in user storage and logs in once with the first code. It does not check that a wrong code is rejected, that a used code cannot be reused, that exhausting all codes forces regeneration, or that the local-DB fallback still works when the user has no federated codes. The reuse and exhaustion gaps are exactly where the user-storage path differs from the local path, so the test would not catch the replay and cleanup problems in this change.
